per_question.question: What are the general eligibility criteria for CAP/DA services under NC Medicaid?
per_question.agent_answer:
The general eligibility criteria for CAP/DA services are that the person must meet both the **general Medicaid coverage standards** for the service and the **program-specific CAP/DA criteria**.

## General CAP/DA eligibility criteria

Under NC Medicaid, CAP/DA is covered when the service is:

- **Individualized, specific, and consistent** with the beneficiary’s symptoms or confirmed diagnosis, and **not more than the beneficiary needs**;
- **Safely furnished**, with **no equally effective and more conservative or less costly treatment available statewide**; and
- **Not primarily for the convenience** of the beneficiary, caretaker, or provider.  
  [[Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment), § 3.1, effective Sept. 1, 2025]

## CAP/DA-specific criteria

NC Medicaid covers CAP/DA when the beneficiary:

- **Meets the required HCBS nursing facility level of care**, as determined by NC Medicaid, and needs long-term care support at a level typically provided in an institution, related to a documented medical diagnosis and functional care need;
- Has a **completed CAP assessment** showing a **reasonable indication** that the person will need at least one CAP/DA HCBS service within **30 calendar days** of the evaluation;
- Has a **signed service plan** authorizing one or more waiver services to be provided **monthly**, to help prevent institutionalization through coordinated case management;
- Or, for short-term equipment/modification/technology needs, has a **signed service plan** authorizing installation needed to return to or remain in the primary private residence and prevent institutional placement, with installation completed within **three calendar months** of service plan approval;
- Is **able to maintain health, safety, and well-being** in the primary private residence or another approved location with formal and informal supports;
- Has paid care needs that can be met **within the average institutional cost** of the CAP/DA waiver;
- Has a **primary physician** who can link and coordinate medical services; and
- Has an **emergency back-up and disaster plan** identifying who will provide care if key staff or a primary caregiver are unavailable or during a public health emergency.  
  [[Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment), § 3.2.1, effective Sept. 1, 2025]

## Important limit

CAP/DA is **not covered** if the beneficiary does not meet the eligibility requirements in Section 2.0 or the criteria in Section 3.0.  
[[Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment), § 4.1, effective Sept. 1, 2025]

per_question.question: What DME items are specifically NOT covered by NC Medicaid under the Orthotics and Prosthetics policy, and what general criteria must be met for coverage?
per_question.agent_answer:
Under NC Medicaid’s **Orthotics & Prosthetics** policy, items are **not covered** if they are primarily for comfort or convenience, are backup/duplicate devices, are for nursing-facility residents, are covered by another agency, or are equipment/supplies for beneficiaries receiving hospice care. For coverage, the item must meet NC Medicaid’s general medical-necessity and eligibility standards and the specific orthotics/prosthetics criteria summarized below. [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

## Items specifically not covered

NC Medicaid’s Orthotics & Prosthetics policy says the following are **not covered**:

- **Devices for the beneficiary’s comfort or convenience**, or for the convenience of the beneficiary’s caregiver(s)
- **Backup devices or duplicates** kept on hand or placed at different locations
- **Devices and supplies for residents of nursing facilities**
- **Devices or supplies covered by another agency**
- **Equipment or supplies for beneficiaries receiving hospice care** [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

## General criteria that must be met for coverage

### Baseline Medicaid coverage criteria

The policy’s general coverage rule requires that the procedure, product, or service be:

- **Individualized, specific, and consistent** with the beneficiary’s symptoms or confirmed diagnosis, and **not in excess of the beneficiary’s needs**
- Able to be **safely furnished**
- Not something for which an **equally effective, more conservative, or less costly treatment** is available statewide
- Furnished in a manner **not primarily intended for the convenience** of the beneficiary, caretaker, or provider [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

### Specific orthotics/prosthetics criteria

In addition, orthotic or prosthetic devices must be:

- **Ordered by a physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner**
- **Medically necessary** to maintain or improve the beneficiary’s medical, physical, or functional level
- **Appropriate for use in a non-institutional setting** where normal life activities take place
- Supported by a **documented face-to-face encounter** with the ordering clinician no more than **6 months** before initiation
- Subject to at least **annual review** of need by the ordering clinician [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

The policy further says:

- **Orthotic devices** are medically necessary when needed to **correct or prevent skeletal deformities**, **support or align movable body parts**, or **preserve or improve physical function**
- **Prosthetic devices** are medically necessary when replacing all or part of the function of a **permanently inoperative, absent, or malfunctioning body part**, and the beneficiary needs the prosthesis for **mobility, daily care, or rehabilitation**
- Orthotic and prosthetic devices must also be:
  - a **reasonable and medically necessary part of the treatment plan**
  - **consistent with the beneficiary’s diagnosis and medical condition**, especially functional limitations and symptoms
  - of **high quality**, with **replacement parts available and obtainable** [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

## Documentation-related requirements

For unlisted adult orthotics/prosthetics requests, the policy’s attachment reiterates that the device must:

- fit the definition of an orthotic or prosthetic
- be **safe, effective, economical**
- be **medical in nature**
- be **generally recognized as an accepted method of treatment**
- **not be experimental or investigational** [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

## Bottom line

A device is generally coverable under Policy 5B only if it is a medically necessary orthotic or prosthetic, properly ordered, clinically appropriate, not for convenience, and not excluded by the specific non-covered categories above. The policy currently appears in the corpus as the authoritative version, and I did not find any separate change notice amending it in the amendment records returned for this document.

per_question.question: What are the entrance, continued service, and discharge criteria for outpatient behavioral health services in NC Medicaid?
per_question.agent_answer:
NC Medicaid covers outpatient behavioral health services only when the beneficiary meets the policy’s coverage criteria; the service is not covered if the beneficiary does not meet Section 3.0 criteria. The current governing policy is effective April 15, 2025. [[8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment), § 4.1]

## Entrance criteria
A beneficiary meets **entrance criteria** for outpatient behavioral health services when all of the following are present:

- A current **DSM-5 diagnosis**;
- Behavioral, psychological, or biological dysfunction and **functional impairment** that are consistent with and associated with the current diagnosis;
- If a higher level of care is indicated but unavailable, or the beneficiary is refusing it, outpatient services may be provided until that higher level of care is available or to support the beneficiary’s participation in that higher level of care;
- The beneficiary is capable of developing skills to manage symptoms, make behavioral changes, and respond favorably to therapeutic interventions; and
- There is no evidence that alternative interventions would be more effective under North Carolina community practice standards. [[8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment), § 3.2.1.1]

## Continued service criteria
For **continued services**, the policy requires:

### First, at least one of these:
- The desired outcome or level of functioning has **not been restored, improved, or sustained** within the timeframe in the treatment plan;
- The beneficiary remains **at risk for relapse** based on current clinical assessment and history; or
- Functional gains are **tenuous**. [[8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment), § 3.2.1.2]

### And, in addition, at least one of these:
- The beneficiary has achieved current treatment plan goals, but **additional goals are indicated** by documented symptoms; or
- The beneficiary is making **satisfactory progress** toward goals, and the documentation supports that continued treatment is warranted. [[8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment), § 3.2.1.2]

## Discharge criteria
A beneficiary meets **discharge criteria** when any of the following applies:

- The beneficiary’s level of functioning has improved with respect to the goals in the treatment plan;
- The beneficiary or legally responsible person no longer wants the services; or
- The beneficiary has not improved despite treatment-plan modifications and needs a **more appropriate best-practice or evidence-based treatment modality** under North Carolina community practice standards. [[8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment), § 3.2.1.3]

## Documentation requirement
The provider’s service record must include:
- an individualized treatment plan, and
- **documentation of entrance criteria, continued service criteria, and discharge criteria**. [[8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment), § 7.3.1]

per_question.question: How does the EPSDT special provision affect coverage for outpatient therapy services, and what ordering practitioner requirements apply to beneficiaries under 21?
per_question.agent_answer:
For NC Medicaid outpatient specialized therapies, the EPSDT special provision can allow a beneficiary under 21 to receive medically necessary therapy services beyond ordinary policy limits, but it does **not** waive prior approval requirements. Also, therapy services for beneficiaries under 21 still require an order before services begin, and the ordering practitioner must be one of the practitioner types listed in Policy 10A. [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), effective Feb. 1, 2025, current]

## EPSDT effect on outpatient therapy coverage

Policy 10A includes an **EPSDT Special Provision** for Medicaid beneficiaries under 21. That provision is tied to **42 U.S.C. § 1396d(r)** and functions as an exception to policy limitations for children and youth under 21. The text also states that EPSDT does **not** require coverage of services that are:
- unsafe,
- ineffective,
- experimental or investigational, or
- not medical in nature or not generally recognized as an accepted method of medical practice or treatment. [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), § 2.2.1, effective Feb. 1, 2025, current]

For prior approval, Policy 10A is explicit: **if a service requires prior approval, being under age 21 does not eliminate that requirement.** [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), “b. EPSDT and Prior Approval Requirements,” effective Feb. 1, 2025, current]

That means, in practice:
- EPSDT may support coverage for medically necessary outpatient therapy for a beneficiary under 21 even when an adult limitation would otherwise apply;
- but the child still must satisfy any applicable **prior approval** requirement.

The policy’s visit-limit sections reinforce this structure. Policy 10A gives fixed annual visit limitations for beneficiaries **21 and older**, while for beneficiaries **under 21** speech-language and audiology therapy are tied to the number of **medically necessary visits within an authorization period**, with the authorization period not exceeding six calendar months. [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), § 5.3 and § 5.4.2, effective Feb. 1, 2025, current]

## Requirements that apply to beneficiaries under 21

For pediatric beneficiaries, the discipline-specific sections in Policy 10A set medical-necessity standards for therapy. For example:
- **Speech-language therapy** includes specific documented findings and pediatric impairment classifications for beneficiaries from birth through age 20. [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), § 3.2.1.3, effective Feb. 1, 2025, current]
- **Audiology therapy (aural rehabilitation)** is covered when the beneficiary demonstrates the qualifying hearing-related deficits and other stated criteria. [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), § 3.2.1.4, effective Feb. 1, 2025, current]

## Ordering practitioner requirements for beneficiaries under 21

Policy 10A identifies the following **ordering practitioners**:
- Medical Doctor (MD)
- Doctor of Osteopathic Medicine (DO)
- Doctor of Podiatric Medicine (DPM)
- Certified Nurse Midwife (CNM)
- Physician Assistant (PA)
- Nurse Practitioner (NP) [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), § 3.1.2, effective Feb. 1, 2025, current]

For treatment services, the policy further requires:
- **a verbal or written order must be obtained before services start**;
- verbal orders must be documented in the beneficiary’s health record and **countersigned by the physician within 60 calendar days**;
- verbal orders are valid for up to **six months** from the documented date of receipt;
- written orders are valid for up to **six months** from the physician’s signature date; and
- **backdating is not allowed**. [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), “Treatment services must adhere to the following requirements,” effective Feb. 1, 2025, current]

## Bottom line

For beneficiaries under 21, EPSDT can expand access to medically necessary outpatient therapy beyond ordinary policy limits, but it **does not remove prior approval requirements**. The child must still meet the policy’s therapy-specific medical-necessity criteria, and treatment must begin only after a valid order from an authorized ordering practitioner. [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), § 2.2.1; “b. EPSDT and Prior Approval Requirements”; § 3.1.2; § 3.2.1.3; § 3.2.1.4; § 5.3; § 5.4.2, effective Feb. 1, 2025, current]

per_question.question: Does NC Medicaid cover Personal Care Services for beneficiaries who live in an assisted living facility?
per_question.agent_answer:
Yes — NC Medicaid does cover Personal Care Services (PCS) for some beneficiaries who live in an assisted living–type setting, but only if they meet the congregate-setting PCS eligibility rules.

## Short answer

For beneficiaries living in a congregate setting, Medicaid covers PCS when the person:

- lives in a qualifying licensed congregate facility, including an **Adult Care Home (ACH)** or certain licensed group homes;
- has a medical, mental, physical, or cognitive condition that creates unmet needs with enough qualifying **activities of daily living (ADLs)**; and
- meets the other medical-necessity and assessment requirements. [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

## What services are covered

In congregate settings, Medicaid covers PCS that occur at least once per week, including:

- hands-on assistance with qualifying ADLs;
- related cueing, prompting, supervision, or guidance when part of that hands-on assistance;
- certain home-management IADLs tied directly to qualifying ADLs and essential to the beneficiary’s care at the private residence;
- assistance with medication, adaptive/assistive devices, durable medical equipment, and certain special assistance/delegated medical monitoring tasks, when the policy conditions are met. [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

## Who qualifies in an assisted living facility

The policy says Medicaid-covered PCS in congregate settings applies to a beneficiary who resides in:

- a congregate facility licensed by North Carolina as an **Adult Care Home**, or
- a **combination home**, or
- certain licensed **group homes**. [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

The beneficiary also must demonstrate unmet need for at least:

- **three of five qualifying ADLs with limited hands-on assistance**, or
- **two ADLs, one requiring extensive assistance**, or
- **two ADLs, one requiring full dependence-level assistance**. [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

Additional required conditions include, among other things:

- the setting must be safe and have required inspection/licensure verification;
- no other third-party payer can be responsible for the PCS;
- no available, willing, and able informal caregiver can provide the authorized services during those times;
- the services must be directly linked to the beneficiary’s documented condition;
- the beneficiary must be under a physician’s ongoing direct care; and
- the beneficiary must be medically stable and not require continuous nursing care, monitoring, or supervision by a licensed professional. [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

## Assessment / authorization requirements

PCS in a congregate facility is not automatic. The policy requires:

- a physician, nurse practitioner, or physician assistant referral/attestation of medical need;
- an independent assessment using the NC Medicaid standardized process; and
- for new admissions, a face-to-face assessment in the beneficiary’s congregate facility. [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

## Practical takeaway

So if by “assisted living facility” you mean a North Carolina licensed **Adult Care Home / assisted living-type congregate facility**, the answer is **yes, potentially** — NC Medicaid can cover PCS there, but only for beneficiaries who satisfy the specific congregate-setting PCS criteria and complete the required assessment process. [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

I checked amendments for both Policy 3L-1 and Policy 3L; the authoritative current congregate-setting source for this question is **Policy 3L-1, State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings**. If you want, I can also pull out the exact rules on **how many hours may be authorized** or **which ADLs count as “qualifying ADLs.”**

per_question.question: Does NC Medicaid cover chiropractic services under Clinical Coverage Policy 5B?
per_question.agent_answer:
No—**Clinical Coverage Policy 5B does not cover chiropractic services as such.** Policy 5B governs **orthotics and prosthetics**, and its coverage criteria are for **devices**, not chiropractic treatment. Covered items must be orthotic or prosthetic devices that are ordered by a physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner and are medically necessary to maintain or improve the beneficiary’s medical, physical, or functional level. [[Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)]

More specifically, Policy 5B says Medicaid covers orthotics and prosthetics when:
- they are **ordered by a physician, PA, or NP**;
- they are **medically necessary**;
- there was a qualifying **face-to-face encounter** within six months before initiation; and
- the need is reviewed at least annually. [[Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)]

The policy also defines covered orthotic devices as those needed to **correct or prevent skeletal deformities, support or align movable body parts, or preserve or improve physical function**. That is device coverage—not coverage of chiropractic manipulation or chiropractic office visits. [[Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)]

One nuance: some orthotic devices in 5B may be furnished by certain licensed professionals listed in the policy’s provider-certification tables, but that does **not** make “chiropractic services” a covered service under 5B. The governing rule is still that the item must qualify as a covered **orthotic or prosthetic device** under the policy. [[Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)]

per_question.question: Can a CAP/DA beneficiary transfer between service providers, and what rules govern transfers of eligible beneficiaries?
per_question.agent_answer:
Yes. A CAP/DA beneficiary can transfer, and the governing rule is the CAP/DA transfer provision in § 3.3. That section requires the Case Management Entity (CME) to coordinate the transfer so there are **no gaps in services**. Under the policy, before a transfer occurs, the CME must complete these steps:

- determine the anticipated start date of service;
- coordinate a transition plan between provider agencies;
- discuss and plan for the beneficiary’s health, safety, and well-being;
- initiate transfer of the electronic health record in the CAP Business System;
- arrange a home visit within **5 business days** after the beneficiary moves to the new primary residence; and
- coordinate services to begin on the **first date of the transfer**.  
  [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment) § 3.3, effective Sept. 1, 2025, current (no amendments identified).

## If the beneficiary is transferring to a different county

Section 3.3 gives more specific rules for county-to-county transfers:

- the transferring CME designee must coordinate with the receiving CME designee on the agreed transfer date or **within less than 30 calendar days of the request to transfer**;
- both CMEs must plan for the beneficiary’s health, safety, and well-being;
- the electronic health record must be transferred to the receiving county;
- the receiving CME must arrange the 5-business-day home visit after the move; and
- services must start on the first day of transfer into the receiving county.  
  [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment) § 3.3, effective Sept. 1, 2025, current.

## Provider choice matters

The CAP/DA service plan rules also support transfers between providers because the beneficiary must be afforded a **right to choose among providers**, documented by a signed freedom-of-choice form. The service plan must identify the authorized provider name, amount, frequency, and duration of each service.  
[Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment) § 5.4.2, effective Sept. 1, 2025, current.

## What I could not verify

I could verify rules for **transfer of eligible CAP/DA beneficiaries**, especially when moving between counties and coordinating services across agencies. per_question.question: Is there a maximum earned income limit for people on HCWD (Health Coverage for Workers with Disabilities), and what premiums apply?
per_question.agent_answer:
No—NC Medicaid policy does **not set a maximum earned income limit** for HCWD. The policy says the limit is on **unearned income**, not earned income: people with **unearned income greater than 150% of the federal poverty level (FPL)** are not eligible for HCWD. It also says HCWD premiums rise with income, and when **countable income exceeds 450% of FPL**, the person pays a **full premium** rather than losing eligibility. [MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf). This MA-2180 policy has been amended, including by [CHANGE NOTICE FOR MANUAL NO. 03-25, 2025 Federal Poverty Level Changes (FPL) Income Changes](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/CN-NO-03-25.docx.pdf), which states the HCWD premium income chart was updated.

## What the policy says about income limits

- **Unearned income cap:** “Those who have unearned incomes greater than 150% of FPL are not eligible for HCWD.” [MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf)
- **No stated earned-income cap:** the same section explains that premiums increase as countable income increases and continue up to a full premium above 450% FPL, rather than stating that earned income over a certain level makes a person ineligible. [MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf)

## Premiums that apply under MA-2180

### General rules
- If **total countable income is 150% FPL or less**: **no cost sharing** other than applicable copayments. [MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf)
- If **total countable income is over 150% FPL**: **$50 annual enrollment fee**. [MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf)
- If **total countable monthly income exceeds 200% FPL**: a **monthly premium** is also due. [MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf)

### Monthly premium chart in MA-2180
Current MA-2180 lists these monthly premiums:

| FPL | Individual income range | Monthly premium | Couple income range | Monthly premium |

Source: [MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf). ## Notice of premium due
NC Medicaid also has an HCWD premium notice form stating that payment is due within 12 days of the letter and instructing the person to make payment to NCDHHS. [dma-5146 Health Coverage for Workers with Disabilities Premium Notice](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/dma-5146.pdf)

per_question.question: What are the requirements for home modifications under CAP/DA, and what documentation must the Multidisciplinary Team provide?
per_question.agent_answer:
Under CAP/DA, home modifications must be tied to the beneficiary’s identified needs and used as part of the approved plan of care. The policy also requires the beneficiary to work with the multidisciplinary team to identify needs for “equipment, modification, technology, training and education and goods and services.” Current source: [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment) (Policy 3K-2, effective Sept. 1, 2025; amendment check completed and this is the current authoritative document).

## Home modification requirements under CAP/DA

The governing rule is that the beneficiary agrees to work collaboratively with the multidisciplinary team to identify needs for modifications and related supports. [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment), “I agree to:”.

More specifically, equipment/modification/technology services must be aimed at one or more of these purposes:

- improving, maximizing, or enhancing the beneficiary’s mobility, safety, or independence;
- improving integration into the community;
- improving environmental and community accessibility; or
- addressing the beneficiary’s 24-hours-a-day, 7-days-a-week coverage concerns.

[Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment), § 3.4.5.

### What kinds of home modifications are contemplated
The policy’s equipment/modification/technology section includes home-related modifications such as:

- ramps, grab bars, safety rails, and handrails;
- widening doorways or passages for wheelchair or walker access;
- medically necessary emergency egress modifications;
- bathroom accessibility modifications;
- bedroom modifications to accommodate hospital beds and wheelchairs;
- kitchen accessibility modifications;
- floor coverings for ease of ambulation;
- certain lifts and related devices;
- door handle and door modifications; and
- replacement of fixtures, mirrors, and storage space when removed or damaged during an approved modification.

The policy also limits covered settings for home modifications to a primary private residence where the beneficiary lives and that is:
- owned by the beneficiary or family;
- a rented residence when the modifications are portable; or
- a rented residence when portable modifications are allowed by the owner.

[Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment), “EQUIPMENT, MODIFICAITON AND TECHNOLOGY.”

## Documentation the Multidisciplinary Team must provide

For equipment, technology, and home modification requests, the policy requires documentation showing the need and supporting the request. The MDT documentation includes:

- **A recommendation by the MDT** identifying the beneficiary’s need for the home modification requested.
- That recommendation **must state the cost** of the item or modification required.
- **A statement of need** identified in the service plan.
- **Evidence of medical need** recommended by the MDT or by a physician, when applicable.
- **A training plan** showing how the beneficiary and family will be trained to use the equipment; the case manager must document completion, and it must be signed by the beneficiary or responsible party.
- **Itemized shipping costs** in the proposal request, if applicable.
- **Other information required for the specific item requested.**
- **Quotes**, when required for purchase, adaptation, or modification; NC Medicaid determines how many quotes are required.
- In special circumstances, **written recommendations from appropriate professionals** as determined by NC Medicaid or its designee.

[Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment), § 5.9.1.

### Additional supporting documentation requirements
Other policy text adds that the request should include:

- a **comprehensive Multidisciplinary declaration of need assessment** completed by the case manager identifying the equipment, supply, adaptation, or modification needs;
- a **copy of the physician’s order**, when applicable;
- a **recommendation by an appropriate professional** identifying the beneficiary’s need for the requested adaptation or modification;
- the **estimated life of the equipment** and the **expected duration of benefit** to the beneficiary; and
- an **invoice from the supplier** showing the date the item/modification was provided and the cost and related charges, maintained in the CAP Business system.

[Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment), “Limits, Amount And Frequency.”

## Bottom line
To qualify, a CAP/DA home modification must address the beneficiary’s functional, safety, accessibility, independence, or round-the-clock care needs and fit within the approved service plan. The MDT must document the need through a recommendation/assessment, connect it to the service plan, support medical necessity when applicable, include cost and quote information, and provide any physician or professional recommendations and training-related documentation required by the policy.

If you want, I can also pull out the **non-covered home modifications/exclusions** or turn this into a short advocacy checklist for an appeal or prior approval request.

per_question.question: How many days of therapeutic leave from a nursing facility does NC Medicaid allow per year, and what conditions must be met?
per_question.agent_answer:
NC Medicaid allows **up to 60 days of therapeutic leave per calendar year** for a resident whose nursing facility bed is already being reimbursed by Medicaid. In addition, **no more than 15 consecutive therapeutic leave days** may be taken **without NC Medicaid approval**. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment), § 5.8, effective Aug. 7, 2024]

## Conditions that must be met

Therapeutic leave from a nursing facility must meet these conditions:

- It must be **for therapeutic purposes only**.
- It must be **ordered by the resident’s attending physician**.
- The **necessity for the leave must be documented in the resident’s plan of care**.
- The **therapeutic justification for each instance** of leave must be entered in the **resident’s health record**.
- The facility must **reserve the resident’s bed** during the absence.
- The facility may receive **Medicaid reimbursement only for that reserved bed**, not other Medicaid revenue for the resident during that leave period.
- The facility must keep a **cumulative record of therapeutic leave days** for audit and reference purposes, and the resident must be listed as on therapeutic leave on the **midnight census**. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment), § 5.8, effective Aug. 7, 2024]

## Important limits

Therapeutic leave is **not available** when the absence is for the purpose of receiving:

- **inpatient services**, or
- **nursing services provided elsewhere or at a different level of care in the current facility**,  

**if Medicaid is paying for those services**. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment), § 5.8, effective Aug. 7, 2024]

Also, **ambulance transportation** to the therapeutic leave site is **not reimbursed** by Medicaid because it is not considered an emergency. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment), § 5.8, effective Aug. 7, 2024]

## Bottom line

**60 days per year**, with **physician-ordered, therapeutically justified leave documented in the care plan and health record**, and **more than 15 consecutive days requires NC Medicaid approval**. The current authoritative document I found is **Clinical Coverage Policy 2B-1, Nursing Facilities**, effective **August 7, 2024**, and I found **no listed amendments** in the amendment record returned for that document.

per_question.question: If a Private Duty Nursing provider terminates services for a Medicaid beneficiary, what notification requirements must they follow?
per_question.agent_answer:
A PDN provider that terminates services must notify **NC Medicaid within 5 business days**, and what they must send depends on why services ended.

## NC Medicaid PDN termination requirements

Under **NC Medicaid Clinical Coverage Policy 3G-1**, section **5.2.4.1, “Notification of Termination”**:

- **If the PDN provider discharges the beneficiary:**  
  the provider must submit the **DMA-3513 (PDN Discharge Summary Form)** to NC Medicaid **within five (5) business days**.  
  Citation: [3G-1 Private Duty Nursing for Beneficiaries Age 21 and Older](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-1-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-age-21-and-older/download?attachment), § 5.2.4.1.

- **If the provider discharges the beneficiary because another source of nursing coverage is available:**  
  the provider must, within **five (5) business days**:
  - **notify NC Medicaid**, and
  - submit the **DMA-3513**.  
  That notification must include:
  - the **last date PDN services were provided and can be billed to Medicaid**, and
  - the **name of the other source of coverage**.  
  Citation: [3G-1 Private Duty Nursing for Beneficiaries Age 21 and Older](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-1-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-age-21-and-older/download?attachment), § 5.2.4.1.

- **If the attending physician terminates PDN services:**  
  the PDN provider must give NC Medicaid, within **five (5) business days**:
  - the **attending physician’s order to terminate PDN services**, and
  - the **DMA-3513**.  
  The policy also says that the decision of the attending physician and/or the PDN provider to discharge the beneficiary **cannot be appealed to NC Medicaid**.  
  Citation: [3G-1 Private Duty Nursing for Beneficiaries Age 21 and Older](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-1-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-age-21-and-older/download?attachment), § 5.2.4.1.

## If termination is due to loss of eligibility or a long break in services

The same section says that if PDN ends because:

- the beneficiary **loses NC Medicaid eligibility**, or
- **no PDN services are provided for 30 consecutive days** for any reason, including hospitalization,

then the **prior approval process must be started again** under sections 5.1 and 5.2.  
Citation: [3G-1 Private Duty Nursing for Beneficiaries Age 21 and Older](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-1-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-age-21-and-older/download?attachment), § 5.2.4.1.

## Written notice and appeal rights

If **NC Medicaid** itself terminates PDN because eligibility, policy criteria, or medical necessity is not met, NC Medicaid (or its designee) must provide the beneficiary/legal representative **written notice of the adverse decision**, including **appeal rights**.  
Citation: [3G-1 Private Duty Nursing for Beneficiaries Age 21 and Older](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-1-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-age-21-and-older/download?attachment), § 5.2.4.1.

For managed care adverse benefit determinations, federal rules require written notice that is timely and adequate, explains the action and reasons, and tells the enrollee about appeal rights and continued benefits rights. See [42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438), §§ 438.404, 438.10.

## Bottom line

For a **provider-initiated PDN termination**, the core NC Medicaid rule is:

- **notify NC Medicaid within 5 business days**, and
- submit the **DMA-3513 discharge form**,
- plus any required extra information such as the **physician’s termination order** or the **other coverage information**, depending on the reason for termination.

I checked amendments for both **3G-1** and **42 CFR Part 438**, and the tool returned those documents as the current authoritative versions for the provisions cited here.

per_question.question: What does federal law define as 'home health services' under Medicaid, and where must they be provided?
per_question.agent_answer:
Under federal Medicaid law, **“home health services”** are the services listed in **42 C.F.R. § 440.70(b)** when they are provided to a beneficiary **at the beneficiary’s place of residence** and under the required practitioner orders and plan-of-care rules. [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)

## What counts as “home health services”
Under **42 C.F.R. § 440.70**, home health services include:

- **Nursing services** provided on a part-time or intermittent basis;
- **Home health aide services**;
- **Medical supplies, equipment, and appliances** suitable for use in settings where normal life activities take place; and
- **Physical therapy, occupational therapy, or speech pathology and audiology services**.  
  These therapy services are optional under the federal home health benefit, while the first three categories are required benefit components. [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)

Federal law also says a state **cannot make home health coverage depend on whether the beneficiary also needs nursing or therapy services**. [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)

## Required ordering and plan-of-care rules
For home health services, federal law requires:

- **Orders written by a physician, nurse practitioner, clinical nurse specialist, or physician assistant**, working in accordance with state law, for the services described in § 440.70(b)(1), (2), and (4);
- Those services must be provided **as part of a written plan of care**; and
- The ordering practitioner must **review the plan of care every 60 days** for those services. [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)

For **medical supplies, equipment, and appliances** under § 440.70(b)(3), the rule uses a slightly different ordering standard: they must be provided on a physician’s order or the order of another licensed practitioner of the healing arts acting within state-law scope of practice, as part of a written plan of care, with review as specified in that subsection. [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)

## Where they must be provided
Federal law says home health services must be provided **at the beneficiary’s place of residence**. [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)

But the regulation also makes clear that a beneficiary’s “place of residence” **does not include**:

- a **hospital**,
- a **nursing facility**, or
- an **intermediate care facility for individuals with intellectual disabilities (ICF/IID)**,

**except** for certain home health services in an ICF/IID that the facility itself is not required to provide. [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)

The rule further states that nothing in § 440.70 allows states to limit home health services only to traditional in-home settings. Instead, they may be provided in **“any setting in which normal life activities take place,”** other than:

- a hospital,
- a nursing facility,
- an ICF/IID, or
- **any setting where Medicaid payment is or could be made for inpatient services that include room and board**. [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)

And importantly, federal law says **home health services cannot be limited to beneficiaries who are homebound**. [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)

## Bottom line
Federal Medicaid law defines home health services as the specified nursing, aide, medical-supply/equipment/appliance, and certain therapy services in **42 C.F.R. § 440.70**, provided under the required orders and written plan of care. They must be furnished at the beneficiary’s **place of residence**, which can include settings where normal life activities occur, but **not** hospitals, nursing facilities, ICFs/IID (with a limited exception), or other inpatient room-and-board settings. [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)

If you want, I can also give you this in a short quote-ready form for a brief or appeal.

per_question.question: How does NC Medicaid define 'terminally ill' for purposes of hospice eligibility, and what certification is required?
per_question.agent_answer:
NC Medicaid hospice policy uses the standard that a beneficiary is **terminally ill if the individual has a life expectancy of six months or less, if the illness runs its normal course**. The policy text I retrieved states this explicitly in the certification materials for continued eligibility and the face-to-face/recertification requirements. See [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment) (effective 2024-03-15), section “D. Certification and Recertification of Terminal Illness,” and section “2. Attestation Statement for Non-Physician Practitioner.”

## Required certification

NC Medicaid requires **written certification of terminal illness for each hospice benefit period**. The hospice provider must obtain the written certification **before submitting a claim for payment**. If the written certification cannot be obtained within two calendar days after a benefit period begins, an **oral certification must be obtained within two calendar days**, with the written certification obtained before the claim is submitted. Certifications may be completed **no more than 15 calendar days before** the effective date of election, and recertifications no more than 15 calendar days before the next benefit period. [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment), § 5.4.1 (effective 2024-03-15).

## What the certification must contain

The certification or recertification must include:

- a physician narrative that briefly synthesizes the clinical information supporting the terminal diagnosis;
- the physician’s attestation that he or she composed the narrative after reviewing the clinical information and, where applicable, examining the beneficiary;
- a narrative reflecting the beneficiary’s individual clinical circumstances;
- the election-period dates to which the certification applies; and
- the certifying or recertifying physician’s signature and date.

For the **third and later election periods**, the narrative must also explain why the clinical findings from the required face-to-face encounter support a life expectancy of six months or less. [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment), section “D. Certification and Recertification of Terminal Illness” (effective 2024-03-15).

## Who must sign it

For the **initial 90-day benefit period**, NC Medicaid requires a written certification statement from:

- the **medical director of the hospice** or the **physician member of the hospice interdisciplinary group (IDG)**; and
- the beneficiary’s **attending physician**, if the beneficiary has one.

For **subsequent benefit periods**, only the **medical director of the hospice** or the **physician member of the hospice interdisciplinary group** must certify. [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment), § 5.4.3 (effective 2024-03-15).

## Face-to-face requirement

A **hospice physician or hospice nurse practitioner** must have a face-to-face encounter with the beneficiary **before, but no more than 30 calendar days before, the third benefit-period recertification and each later recertification**, to gather clinical findings for continued hospice eligibility. But a non-physician practitioner may not certify terminal illness; if a Medicare-recognized non-physician provider performed the encounter, the attestation must say the findings were given to the certifying physician for the determination whether the beneficiary continues to have a life expectancy of six months or less. [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment), § 5.4.1 and section “2. Attestation Statement for Non-Physician Practitioner” (effective 2024-03-15).

per_question.question: What ambulance services are NOT covered by NC Medicaid?
per_question.agent_answer:
NC Medicaid does **not** cover ambulance services that fall outside the policy’s covered-service criteria, and it specifically excludes several listed situations and charges.

## General non-covered rule
Under the Ambulance Services policy, ambulance services are not covered if:

- the beneficiary does not meet Medicaid eligibility requirements,
- the beneficiary does not meet the ambulance coverage criteria,
- the service duplicates another provider’s service, or
- the service is experimental, investigational, or part of a clinical trial.  
Cite: [Ambulance Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment), § 4.1, effective 12/15/2023 (current; no later amendment identified through amendment check).

## Specific ambulance services and charges NC Medicaid does not cover
The policy specifically says NC Medicaid does **not** cover:

- **Loaded mileage to a facility that is not the nearest appropriate facility**  
  If the beneficiary is transported to a facility that is not the nearest appropriate facility, that loaded mileage is not reimbursed. The policy also says beneficiary preference, or whether a physician has staff privileges at a hospital, does not determine whether a facility is “appropriate.”  
  Cite: [Ambulance Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment), § 4.2.1.1, effective 12/15/2023.

- **An ambulance call where no treatment is needed**
- **False alarm responses**
- **Situations where the beneficiary refuses all medical services**
- **Ambulance transport for a medical service that is not itself a Medicaid-covered service**
- **Commercial airline tickets**
- **Airstrip fees**
- **Taxes charged separately** (local, state, federal, etc.)
- **Separate additional charges for nursing personnel** who are employees of a facility or ambulance service
- **Waiting fees**
- **Separate charges for oxygen and other items/supplies**, because those are included in the base rate and are not separately reimbursable
- **Any services other than those listed in Subsection 3.2**  
  Cite: [Ambulance Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment), § 4.2.1 and § 4.2.1.4, effective 12/15/2023.

## Coverage baseline for context
The policy’s coverage rule is that Medicaid covers ambulance **emergency services** to the extent necessary to screen and stabilize the beneficiary, without prior authorization when a prudent layperson would reasonably believe an emergency medical condition existed. Payment is based on retrospective review of the presenting history and symptoms. So if a claimed ambulance service falls outside those covered criteria, it may be non-covered.  
Cite: [Ambulance Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment), § 3.2 and § 3.2.1, effective 12/15/2023.

per_question.question: Are there quantity limits on prescription drugs under NC Medicaid, and when is prior authorization required for pharmacy claims?
per_question.agent_answer:
Yes. Under NC Medicaid Policy **9**, outpatient pharmacy claims are subject to **quantity-related limits**, and **prior authorization (PA)** is required for certain drugs and situations.

## 1) Quantity limits

NC Medicaid Policy 9 expressly addresses **“Dispensing and Maximum Supply”** and includes a section on **“Quantity and Episodic Drugs.”** That section refers to:
- evaluating the applicability of **quantity limitations** for episodic drugs,
- **prior authorization criteria and requirements**, and
- actions to minimize dispensing fees for drugs prescribed in limited quantities.  
Citations: [Lock-in Program](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/9-outpatient-pharmacy-program/download?attachment), § 5.4.3 “Quantity and Episodic Drugs” (effective July 15, 2024; current per amendment check).

The policy also shows quantity-related claim edits through its DUR/early refill rules. For example:
- an early refill alert may occur when the previous prescription has **more than 25% of days’ supply remaining**; and
- certain early refill override codes are limited, such as one vacation-supply occurrence per 365 days for non-controlled medications and one lost-prescription occurrence on one date of service per 365 days for non-controlled medications.  
Citations: [Lock-in Program](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/9-outpatient-pharmacy-program/download?attachment), “G.7 DUR Alert Message Examples”; “Approved Prescription Clarification Codes for Early Refill” (effective July 15, 2024; current per amendment check).

So the safest answer is: **yes, NC Medicaid imposes quantity-related limits, including quantity limitations for some drugs and refill timing/day-supply edits.** The specific limit depends on the drug/edit involved.

## 2) When prior authorization is required

Under Policy **9**, PA is required for drugs that NC Medicaid places in its **Pharmacy Prior Approval Drugs and Criteria** list. The policy includes a dedicated section listing drug categories/products subject to PA, such as:
- GLP-1 receptor agonists and combinations
- Hepatitis C medications
- Growth hormones
- PCSK9 inhibitors
- Opioid analgesics
- Sedative hypnotics
- Triptans
- Synagis
- CGM systems and related supplies
- and many other named classes/products.  
Citation: [Lock-in Program](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/9-outpatient-pharmacy-program/download?attachment), “Pharmacy Prior Approval Drugs and Criteria” / Attachment K (effective July 15, 2024; current per amendment check).

Policy 9 also states under **5.1 Prior Authorization** that PA is used for:
- **new variations** of products already in the marketplace,
- **new indications** for products already in the marketplace,
- **changes in indications**, and
- **changes in dosing** for products already in the marketplace.  
Citation: [Lock-in Program](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/9-outpatient-pharmacy-program/download?attachment), § 5.1 “Prior Authorization” (within § 5.0; effective July 15, 2024; current per amendment check).

## 3) If the request is outside usual criteria

Policy 9, § **3.2.3**, addresses exceptions to FDA and NC Medicaid drug criteria approval. For an exception request, the policy requires support such as:
- health record information showing **medical necessity**,
- explanation of what other drugs were tried or why they cannot be tried,
- explanation from the prescriber why FDA-approved guidelines/evidence-based standards or NC Medicaid drug criteria are insufficient, and
- supporting compendia or peer-reviewed literature.  
Citation: [Lock-in Program](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/9-outpatient-pharmacy-program/download?attachment), § 3.2.3 “Exceptions to FDA and NC Medicaid Drug criteria approval” (effective July 15, 2024; current per amendment check).

## Bottom line

- **Quantity limits:** **Yes.** NC Medicaid pharmacy policy includes quantity limitations for some drugs, plus refill/day-supply edits and related restrictions.
- **Prior authorization:** **Required when the drug or drug category is listed in Policy 9’s Pharmacy Prior Approval Drugs and Criteria / Attachment K, and in certain new-product/new-indication/dosing-change situations.**
- **Exception requests:** May be approved if the prescriber documents medical necessity and supporting evidence under § 3.2.3.

per_question.question: Under what conditions can speech therapy be provided via telehealth under NC Medicaid?
per_question.agent_answer:
Speech therapy may be provided via telehealth under NC Medicaid only in limited circumstances and subject to specific safeguards.

## NC Medicaid rule

NC Medicaid says that **only a select set of speech and language evaluation and treatment interventions** may be delivered by telehealth, and they must be provided **as described in Clinical Coverage Policy 1H**. Telehealth **may be medically necessary** when:

- the beneficiary’s medical condition is such that **exposure to others should be avoided**, or
- the beneficiary is in a **remote or underserved location** where access to appropriately qualified providers is limited.

NC Medicaid also requires all of the following when deciding whether speech therapy should be delivered by telehealth:

- **Unless in-person care is contraindicated or unavailable, telehealth must be used as an adjunct to in-person care and not as a replacement.**
- Telehealth must be used **in the beneficiary’s best interest**, **not as a convenience for the therapist**.
- Telehealth must **never** be used **solely to increase therapist productivity**.  
  [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment) (effective Feb. 1, 2025), section “e. Telehealth”

## Other speech-therapy coverage conditions still apply

Telehealth does not eliminate the ordinary coverage rules for outpatient speech-language pathology services. Federal rules still require that outpatient speech-language pathology services be:

- furnished while the beneficiary is **under the care of a physician**;
- furnished under a **written plan of treatment** meeting the applicable plan requirements; and
- furnished by a qualified speech-language pathologist or other permitted provider arrangement.  
  [42 CFR Part 410](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-410), § 410.62

## Telehealth modality

The federal telehealth regulation generally describes telehealth services as requiring an **interactive telecommunications system** with **two-way, real-time audio and video**, though in some circumstances it can include **two-way, real-time audio-only communication** for services furnished to a patient in the home when the practitioner is technically capable of video but the patient cannot use or does not consent to video.  
[42 CFR Part 410](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-410), § 410.78

## Bottom line

Under NC Medicaid, speech therapy can be provided via telehealth when:

1. the service is one of the **select speech/language interventions allowed for telehealth**;
2. telehealth is **medically necessary**, such as to avoid exposure risk or because the beneficiary is in a remote/underserved area with limited provider access;
3. telehealth is used **as a supplement to in-person care**, unless in-person care is contraindicated or unavailable;
4. it is used **for the beneficiary’s benefit**, not therapist convenience or productivity; and
5. the usual speech-therapy coverage requirements, including qualified provider and plan-of-treatment requirements, are still met.

per_question.question: What medical loss ratio (MLR) must Medicaid managed care organizations meet under federal law, and how does NC implement this requirement?
per_question.agent_answer:
Under federal Medicaid managed care law, plans must **calculate and report** an MLR, but a plan is not automatically subject to a universal federal minimum unless the state chooses to impose one. If a state does impose a minimum MLR, that minimum must be **at least 85%**. In other words, **85% is the floor for any state-imposed minimum**, not an across-the-board federal minimum that applies in every state by itself. [42 CFR Part 438, § 438.8](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

## Federal rule

42 C.F.R. § 438.8 says:

- The state must ensure through its managed care contracts that each **MCO, PIHP, and PAHP calculate and report an MLR**. [42 CFR Part 438, § 438.8(a)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)
- **If** the state elects to require a minimum MLR, that minimum **“must be equal to or higher than 85 percent.”** [42 CFR Part 438, § 438.8(c)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

So the federal rule has two separate parts:

1. **Unconditional duty:** plans must calculate and report MLR.
2. **Conditional minimum-threshold rule:** if the state mandates a minimum MLR, it cannot be lower than **85%**.

## How North Carolina implements it

North Carolina’s implementation evidence in the retrieved NC material is limited, but it does show that the state has built MLR compliance into its managed care framework and remittance reporting.

The NC state plan amendment material says:

- The state assures its rates are designed to **reasonably achieve a medical loss ratio**. [SPA 22-0013 Proposed Amendments CHIP-Managed Care, § 3.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/22-0013-proposed-amendment-chip-managed-care/download?attachment)
- If an MCO, PIHP, or PAHP owes a **remittance** for not meeting the **minimum MLR required by the State**, NC will:
  - reimburse CMS for the federal share of the remittance; and
  - submit a separate report describing the state/federal share methodology with the annual report to CMS. [SPA 22-0013 Proposed Amendments CHIP-Managed Care, § 3.3.5](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/22-0013-proposed-amendment-chip-managed-care/download?attachment)

That means NC’s implementation, at least in the material retrieved here, includes:

- designing rates to reasonably achieve the target MLR; and
- requiring financial reconciliation/remittance reporting if a plan fails to meet the state-required minimum MLR.

## Bottom line

- **Federal law:** Medicaid managed care plans must calculate and report MLR; any state-imposed minimum MLR must be **at least 85%**. [42 CFR Part 438, § 438.8](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)
- **North Carolina:** the retrieved NC source indicates the state structures rates to achieve MLR and has a remittance/reporting process when a plan fails to meet the **state-required minimum MLR**. [SPA 22-0013 Proposed Amendments CHIP-Managed Care, § 3.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/22-0013-proposed-amendment-chip-managed-care/download?attachment)

I could not verify from the retrieved NC text alone whether NC expressly states, in the specific source we pulled, the exact numeric minimum as **85%** in that state document itself, even though that is the federal floor for any state-mandated minimum.  

**Amendment status checked:** no amendments were returned for either [42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438) or [SPA 22-0013 Proposed Amendments CHIP-Managed Care](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/22-0013-proposed-amendment-chip-managed-care/download?attachment).

per_question.question: What are the specific criteria for NC Medicaid coverage of CAR-T cell therapy?
per_question.agent_answer:
NC Medicaid covers CAR-T cell therapy when the beneficiary meets the policy’s general coverage standards and the therapy meets the policy’s CAR-T-specific requirements. In particular, the CAR-T product must be FDA-approved, used according to FDA-approved guidelines, and administered at a certified or authorized treatment center; if the product is subject to an FDA-required REMS program, the treatment center must be enrolled in that REMS and providers must be trained to manage cytokine release syndrome and neurologic toxicities. The current governing policy is effective April 1, 2025, and I did not find a separate amendment superseding it. [CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

## Specific NC Medicaid coverage criteria for CAR-T cell therapy

### 1. General coverage criteria must be met
NC Medicaid requires that the service be:

- individualized, specific, and consistent with the beneficiary’s symptoms or confirmed diagnosis, and not in excess of the beneficiary’s needs;
- safely furnished, with no equally effective and more conservative or less costly treatment available statewide; and
- furnished in a manner not primarily intended for the convenience of the beneficiary, caretaker, or provider. [CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

### 2. CAR-T-specific criteria must be met
For CAR-T cell therapy specifically, Medicaid covers it only if:

- the CAR-T therapy has received approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration;
- the therapy is administered according to U.S. FDA-approved guidelines for:
  - indications and usage,
  - dosage and administration,
  - dosage forms and strengths, and
  - warnings and precautions; and
- the therapy is administered at a certified or authorized treatment center.

If the therapy is subject to a Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategies (REMS) program, then:

- the treatment center must be enrolled in that REMS program; and
- providers must be trained on management of cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and neurologic toxicities. [CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

## When NC Medicaid will not cover it
The policy also makes clear that CAR-T is not covered if, among other things:

- the beneficiary does not meet the eligibility requirements in Section 2.0;
- the beneficiary does not meet the criteria in Section 3.0;
- the service duplicates another provider’s service; or
- the service is experimental, investigational, or part of a clinical trial. [CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

More specifically, CAR-T is not covered if:

- the product is not FDA-approved;
- it is administered outside FDA guidelines for indications/usage, dosage/administration, or dosage forms/strengths;
- a CAR-T that requires REMS is administered at a facility not enrolled in that REMS program;
- it is a repeat treatment in a beneficiary who previously received another CAR-T therapy;
- the beneficiary’s psychosocial history limits the ability to comply with pre- and post-infusion care; or
- current beneficiary or caretaker non-compliance makes adherence to a disciplined medical regimen improbable. [CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

## Prior-approval documentation tied to coverage
Although you asked about coverage criteria, the policy also identifies documentation NC Medicaid expects for approval, which often matters in practice:

- a letter of medical necessity signed by the attending physician documenting past chemotherapy regimens and dates, clinical and social history, and indications for CAR-T treatment;
- verification that the administering facility is a qualified or authorized treatment center for the requested CAR-T product;
- HIV and hepatitis serologies less than three months old, with some allowance for older positive serology results;
- diagnostic and procedure results, including bone marrow biopsy not more than six months old;
- any other diagnostic tests requested as appropriate; and
- a complete psychological and social evaluation addressing compliance, support network, post-treatment care plan, and history of mental health, substance use, or legal issues. [CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

## Bottom line
The core test is:

1. the beneficiary meets NC Medicaid’s general medical-necessity-style coverage rules;
2. the CAR-T product is FDA-approved and used exactly within FDA-approved parameters; and
3. the therapy is provided at the properly certified/authorized center, with REMS compliance when required. [CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

per_question.question: Can an NC Innovations waiver participant request services that exceed their individual base budget, and what happens if they believe their needs cannot be met within the budget?
per_question.agent_answer:
Yes. An NC Innovations participant may request services that cost more than their individual base budget, and the base budget is not a binding cap on what can be authorized.

## Short answer

If the participant believes their needs cannot be met within the base budget, they can request additional services. NC Medicaid policy says the SIS results and base budget are only **guidelines** and **do not constitute a binding limit** on the amount of services that may be requested or authorized. If the LME/MCO determines the services are **medically necessary**, they are to be authorized **regardless of the base budget**. If the request is denied, the participant must be told the reasons and how to appeal, and they may also file a grievance regarding the base budget. [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment) (effective 2016-11-01, current), “Category Assignment and Individual Budget Changes.”

## What the governing rules say

### 1) Federal HCBS rules require services to be based on assessed need and the person-centered plan
Under the HCBS waiver rules, services must be provided under a **written person-centered service plan** based on a person-centered approach and approved by the Medicaid agency. The plan must reflect the services and supports needed to address the person’s assessed functional needs, within the scope of services available under the waiver. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441), § 441.301 (current).

That means the waiver operates through an individualized service plan tied to assessed need, not just a preset budget figure.

### 2) NC Innovations expressly allows requests above the base budget
NC Innovations policy states:

- the individual **“may request services that cost in excess of his or her base budget if he or she believes his or her needs cannot be met within his or her base budget”**;  
- the SIS results and base budget are **guidelines** only, not a binding limit; and  
- if the LME/MCO determines the services are **medically necessary, they will be authorized, regardless of the base budget**.  
See [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment) (effective 2016-11-01, current), “Category Assignment and Individual Budget Changes.”

## What happens if the participant says the budget is not enough?

According to NC Innovations policy, if the participant believes the base budget is insufficient:

- they can **request services above the base budget**;
- the LME/MCO must evaluate whether those services are **medically necessary**;
- if approved, the services may be authorized **even if they exceed the budget**;
- if denied, the participant must receive notice of:
  - **the reasons for the denial**,
  - **how to appeal**, and
  - **how to file a grievance regarding the base budget**.  
See [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment) (effective 2016-11-01, current), “Category Assignment and Individual Budget Changes.”

## Related practical point from the policy

NC Innovations also contains service-authorization language showing that higher levels of service can be authorized for set periods, and if extended authorization is needed, review is based on **medical necessity** and the treatment team should review sustainable supports, including both waiver and non-waiver options. See [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment) (effective 2016-11-01, current), “NC Medicaid North Carolina Innovations.”

I can verify from the policy that the participant may request services above the base budget and that medical necessity can override the base budget.
